proof_summary: For every odd prime divisor \(p\) of a composite \(n=pc\), Fermat’s theorem makes the factors indexed by multiples of \(p-1\) provide more powers of \(p\) than occur in \((n-1)!\), forcing \(p\mid a(n-1)\) and hence the impossible \(p\mid 2^{n-2}\); if \(n=2^e\), the oddness of the product and Legendre’s binary digit-sum formula give \(v_2(a(2^e-1))=e-1\), yielding the analogous contradiction. Thus \(n\) is prime, and if the order \(d\) of \(2\bmod n\) were less than \(n-1\), the factor \(2^d-1\) would survive division by \((n-1)!\) and force \(n\mid a(n-1)\), again contradicting that an odd prime cannot divide \(2^{n-2}\); hence the order is \(n-1\).
